newsitem.title: USA: Blizzard dies down in U.S. plains, cold moves in.
newsitem.headline: Blizzard dies down in U.S. plains, cold moves in.

text.p: A blinding blizzard that stranded scores of motorists across the Great Plains began to die out on Wednesday but most schools and shops remained closed as bone-chilling wind made going outside dangerous.

Temperatures below freezing accompanied by 60 mile-per-hour (100 km per hour) wind gusts made travel hazardous and drifting snow kept highways shut across much of the eastern half of the Dakotas and northwest Minnesota.

"It's still blowing but it's not that bad. The (shopping) mall is opening back up," secretary Sharon Fletcher at the mayor's office in Fargo said. "It had to be pretty bad for the mall to shut down during the Christmas season."

There were dozens of road accidents in North Dakota but no fatalities and motorists had to be rescued from snowdrifts beneath highway overpasses and at rest stops, Sgt. Mark Bethke of the state Highway Patrol said. An icy storm in Oklahoma on Tuesday caused six traffic deaths in that state.
The National Weather Service said sub-freezing temperatures extended south as far at the U.S.-Mexico border, and a rare snowfall was forecast for Louisiana.

"The Dakotas, Minnesota, and Iowa will experience high winds for another day since this storm is slow to move east," the Weather Service's Todd Heitkamp said. He said the East Coast should feel the impact of snow and cold by the weekend.

North Dakota had already received half its normal winter allotment of 26 inches (66 cm) of snow and winter has not yet officially begun, Heitkamp said. It was the snowiest autumn since 1982 and Heitkamp said the "ground blizzard" was caused in part by blowing and drifting of snow already on the ground.

White-out conditions stranded motorists in cars and some people have spent consecutive nights in crowded motels and in school gymnasiums. Snow ploughs were starting to clear roads in the western Dakotas.
On the heels of the blizzard, temperatures were expected to fall to minus 20 (minus 29 Celsius) in North Dakota.
"It's still blustery but we're kind of used to this bad weather," Fletcher said.
